claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans, ablation of germline stem cells (GSCs) extends lifespan.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, ablation of germline stem cells (GSCs) extends lifespan, but also increases fat accumulation and alters lipid metabolism, raising the intriguing question of how these effects might be related.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript to previous work (Hsin and Kenyon, 1999; Arantes-Oliveira et al., 2002).

claim: Ablation of germline stem cells increases fat accumulation in C. elegans.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, ablation of germline stem cells (GSCs) extends lifespan, but also increases fat accumulation and alters lipid metabolism, raising the intriguing question of how these effects might be related.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5 showing increased ORO staining in glp-1(ts) animals, as well as citations to previous work (O'Rourke et al., 2009).

claim: Ablation of germline stem cells alters lipid metabolism in C. elegans.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, ablation of germline stem cells (GSCs) extends lifespan, but also increases fat accumulation and alters lipid metabolism, raising the intriguing question of how these effects might be related.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 5A showing altered expression of lipid metabolism genes, as well as citations to previous work (Wang et al., 2008; Goudeau et al., 2011).

claim: A lack of GSCs results in a broad transcriptional reprogramming in C. elegans.
source: Here, we show that a lack of GSCs results in a broad transcriptional reprogramming in which the conserved detoxification regulator SKN-1/Nrf increases stress resistance, proteasome activity, and longevity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 3 showing 1306 genes upregulated more than fourfold in GSC(-) animals.

claim: SKN-1/Nrf increases stress resistance in response to GSC absence.
source: Here, we show that a lack of GSCs results in a broad transcriptional reprogramming in which the conserved detoxification regulator SKN-1/Nrf increases stress resistance, proteasome activity, and longevity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1C-F showing that skn-1 is required for GSC(-) animals to exhibit increased oxidative stress resistance.

claim: SKN-1/Nrf increases proteasome activity in response to GSC absence.
source: Here, we show that a lack of GSCs results in a broad transcriptional reprogramming in which the conserved detoxification regulator SKN-1/Nrf increases stress resistance, proteasome activity, and longevity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4C,D showing that skn-1 is required for increased proteasome activity in GSC(-) animals.

claim: SKN-1/Nrf increases longevity in response to GSC absence.
source: Here, we show that a lack of GSCs results in a broad transcriptional reprogramming in which the conserved detoxification regulator SKN-1/Nrf increases stress resistance, proteasome activity, and longevity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1A,B showing that skn-1 is required for lifespan extension in glp-1(ts) animals.

claim: SKN-1 activates diverse lipid metabolism genes in response to GSC absence.
source: SKN-1 also activates diverse lipid metabolism genes and reduces fat storage, thereby alleviating the increased fat accumulation caused by GSC absence.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 5A showing SKN-1-dependent upregulation of lipid metabolism genes.

claim: SKN-1 reduces fat storage in response to GSC absence.
source: SKN-1 also activates diverse lipid metabolism genes and reduces fat storage, thereby alleviating the increased fat accumulation caused by GSC absence.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5B,C showing that skn-1 mutants have increased ORO staining compared to wild-type and glp-1(ts) animals.

claim: SKN-1 alleviates the increased fat accumulation caused by GSC absence.
source: SKN-1 also activates diverse lipid metabolism genes and reduces fat storage, thereby alleviating the increased fat accumulation caused by GSC absence.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5B,C showing that glp-1(ts);skn-1 double mutants have higher fat levels than glp-1(ts) single mutants.

claim: SKN-1 is activated by signals from fat in GSC(-) animals.
source: Surprisingly, SKN-1 is activated by signals from this fat, which appears to derive from unconsumed yolk that was produced for reproduction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6 showing that SKN-1 activation in GSC(-) animals requires lipogenesis (sbp-1), FA desaturation (fat-6/7), and lipid transport (lbp-8), and can be rescued by oleic acid supplementation.

claim: The fat that accumulates in GSC(-) animals appears to derive from unconsumed yolk that was produced for reproduction.
source: Surprisingly, SKN-1 is activated by signals from this fat, which appears to derive from unconsumed yolk that was produced for reproduction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6A,B showing dramatic accumulation of VIT-2::GFP (yolk lipoprotein) in GSC(-) animals.

claim: SKN-1 plays a direct role in maintaining lipid homeostasis in which it is activated by lipids.
source: We conclude that SKN-1 plays a direct role in maintaining lipid homeostasis in which it is activated by lipids.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing SKN-1 regulates lipid metabolism genes and is activated by lipid signals.

claim: The SKN-1 function in lipid homeostasis may explain the importance of mammalian Nrf proteins in fatty liver disease.
source: This SKN-1 function may explain the importance of mammalian Nrf proteins in fatty liver disease and suggest that particular endogenous or dietary lipids might promote health through SKN-1/Nrf.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a speculation based on the findings about SKN-1's role in lipid homeostasis and existing knowledge about Nrf proteins in NAFLD.

claim: Particular endogenous or dietary lipids might promote health through SKN-1/Nrf.
source: This SKN-1 function may explain the importance of mammalian Nrf proteins in fatty liver disease and suggest that particular endogenous or dietary lipids might promote health through SKN-1/Nrf.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a speculation based on the findings that SKN-1 is activated by specific lipids like oleic acid and that this activation promotes beneficial outcomes.

claim: GSC loss increases lifespan in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: GSC loss also increases lifespan in Drosophila melanogaster (Flatt et al., 2008), and castration has been associated with longevity in men (Min et al., 2012), suggesting that this relationship might be conserved.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Flatt et al., 2008.

claim: Castration has been associated with longevity in men.
source: GSC loss also increases lifespan in Drosophila melanogaster (Flatt et al., 2008), and castration has been associated with longevity in men (Min et al., 2012), suggesting that this relationship might be conserved.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Min et al., 2012.

claim: The relationship between GSC loss and longevity might be conserved across species.
source: GSC loss also increases lifespan in Drosophila melanogaster (Flatt et al., 2008), and castration has been associated with longevity in men (Min et al., 2012), suggesting that this relationship might be conserved.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference based on observations in C. elegans, Drosophila, and humans.

claim: DAF-16/FOXO is needed for longevity from GSC ablation.

evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Lin et al., 2001; Libina et al., 2003; Kenyon, 2010.

claim: DAF-16/FOXO is regulated differently by GSC ablation and reduced insulin/IGF-1 signaling.
source: DAF-16/FOXO is needed for longevity from GSC ablation or reduced insulin/IGF-1 signaling (IIS) but is regulated differently by each pathway (Lin et al., 2001; Libina et al., 2003; Kenyon, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Lin et al., 2001; Libina et al., 2003; Kenyon, 2010.

claim: GSC(-) longevity requires PHA-4/FOXA.

evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: GSC(-) longevity requires the nuclear receptor DAF-12/FXR.
source: GSC(−) longevity also requires HLH-30/TFEB, PHA-4/FOXA, and the nuclear receptors DAF-12/FXR, NHR-80/HNF4, and NHR-49/PPARα (Hsin and Kenyon, 1999; Goudeau et al., 2011; Lapierre et al., 2011; O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013; Ratnappan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

source: GSC(−) longevity also requires HLH-30/TFEB, PHA-4/FOXA, and the nuclear receptors DAF-12/FXR, NHR-80/HNF4, and NHR-49/PPARα (Hsin and Kenyon, 1999; Goudeau et al., 2011; Lapierre et al., 2011; O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013; Ratnappan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

source: GSC(−) longevity also requires HLH-30/TFEB, PHA-4/FOXA, and the nuclear receptors DAF-12/FXR, NHR-80/HNF4, and NHR-49/PPARα (Hsin and Kenyon, 1999; Goudeau et al., 2011; Lapierre et al., 2011; O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013; Ratnappan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Under most conditions, GSC(-) longevity depends upon a hormonal signal from the somatic gonad that activates DAF-12.
source: Under most conditions, GSC(−) longevity also depends upon a hormonal signal from the somatic gonad that activates DAF-12 (Kenyon, 2010; Antebi, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Kenyon, 2010; Antebi, 2013.

claim: During aging, GSC(-) animals maintain more robust responses to thermal and proteotoxic stress.
source: During aging, GSC(−) animals maintain more robust responses to thermal and proteotoxic stress (Ben-Zvi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Ben-Zvi et al., 2009.

claim: GSC(-) animals exhibit a striking daf-16-dependent increase in activity of the proteasome.
source: They also exhibit a striking daf-16-dependent increase in activity of the proteasome (Vilchez et al., 2012), a multisubunit complex which degrades proteins that the ubiquitylation system has tagged for decay (Glickman and Ciechanover, 2002; Goldberg, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Vilchez et al., 2012.

claim: GSC removal enhances immunity.
source: In addition, GSC removal enhances immunity (Alper et al., 2010) and boosts oxidative stress resistance through an undetermined DAF-16-independent mechanism (Libina et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Alper et al., 2010.

claim: GSC removal boosts oxidative stress resistance through an undetermined DAF-16-independent mechanism.
source: In addition, GSC removal enhances immunity (Alper et al., 2010) and boosts oxidative stress resistance through an undetermined DAF-16-independent mechanism (Libina et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Libina et al., 2003.

claim: Expression of particular fatty acid oxidation genes is increased in GSC(-) animals.
source: Expression of particular fatty acid (FA) oxidation, FA desaturation, and triglyceride lipase genes is increased, as is total lipase activity (Wang et al., 2008; Goudeau et al., 2011; Lapierre et al., 2011; McCormick et al., 2012; Ratnappan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Expression of particular FA desaturation genes is increased in GSC(-) animals.
source: Expression of particular fatty acid (FA) oxidation, FA desaturation, and triglyceride lipase genes is increased, as is total lipase activity (Wang et al., 2008; Goudeau et al., 2011; Lapierre et al., 2011; McCormick et al., 2012; Ratnappan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Expression of particular triglyceride lipase genes is increased in GSC(-) animals.
source: Expression of particular fatty acid (FA) oxidation, FA desaturation, and triglyceride lipase genes is increased, as is total lipase activity (Wang et al., 2008; Goudeau et al., 2011; Lapierre et al., 2011; McCormick et al., 2012; Ratnappan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Production of the unsaturated free FA oleic acid is required for GSC(-) longevity.
source: Production of the unsaturated free FA (FFA) oleic acid (OA) is required (Goudeau et al., 2011), as are the triglyceride lipases LIPL-4/LIPA and FARD-1/FAR2 (Wang et al., 2008; McCormick et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Goudeau et al., 2011.

claim: The triglyceride lipase LIPL-4/LIPA is required for GSC(-) longevity.
source: Production of the unsaturated free FA (FFA) oleic acid (OA) is required (Goudeau et al., 2011), as are the triglyceride lipases LIPL-4/LIPA and FARD-1/FAR2 (Wang et al., 2008; McCormick et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Wang et al., 2008; McCormick et al., 2012.

claim: The triglyceride lipase FARD-1/FAR2 is required for GSC(-) longevity.
source: Production of the unsaturated free FA (FFA) oleic acid (OA) is required (Goudeau et al., 2011), as are the triglyceride lipases LIPL-4/LIPA and FARD-1/FAR2 (Wang et al., 2008; McCormick et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Wang et al., 2008; McCormick et al., 2012.

claim: SKN-1 is orthologous to the mammalian Nrf1/2/3 proteins.
source: The C. elegans transcription factor SKN-1 controls a broad detoxification response to oxidative and xenobiotic stress and is orthologous to the mammalian Nrf1/2/3 (NF-E2-related factor) proteins (An and Blackwell, 2003; Oliveira et al., 2009; Park et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to An and Blackwell, 2003; Oliveira et al., 2009; Park et al., 2009.

claim: SKN-1 controls a broad detoxification response to oxidative and xenobiotic stress.
source: The C. elegans transcription factor SKN-1 controls a broad detoxification response to oxidative and xenobiotic stress and is orthologous to the mammalian Nrf1/2/3 (NF-E2-related factor) proteins (An and Blackwell, 2003; Oliveira et al., 2009; Park et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to An and Blackwell, 2003; Oliveira et al., 2009; Park et al., 2009.

claim: SKN-1/Nrf proteins have been implicated in longevity from C. elegans to rodents.
source: SKN-1/Nrf proteins have been implicated in longevity from C. elegans to rodents (An and Blackwell, 2003; Bishop and Guarente, 2007; Leiser and Miller, 2010; Sykiotis and Bohmann, 2010; Steinbaugh et al., 2012; Ewald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: SKN-1/Nrf proteins influence expression of lipid metabolism genes.
source: SKN-1/Nrf proteins influence expression of lipid metabolism genes (Oliveira et al., 2009; Paek et al., 2012; Hayes and Dinkova-Kostova, 2014; Tsujita et al., 2014), and SKN-1 has been linked to fat mobilization under particular starvation or dietary conditions (Paek et al., 2012; Pang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: SKN-1 has been linked to fat mobilization under particular starvation or dietary conditions.
source: SKN-1/Nrf proteins influence expression of lipid metabolism genes (Oliveira et al., 2009; Paek et al., 2012; Hayes and Dinkova-Kostova, 2014; Tsujita et al., 2014), and SKN-1 has been linked to fat mobilization under particular starvation or dietary conditions (Paek et al., 2012; Pang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Paek et al., 2012; Pang et al., 2014.

claim: Mice that lack Nrf1 in the liver develop non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) that progresses to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).
source: Mice that lack Nrf1 in the liver develop non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) that progresses to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), and Nrf2−/− mice develop NASH on a high-fat diet (Xu et al., 2005; Okada et al., 2013; Tsujita et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Xu et al., 2005; Okada et al., 2013; Tsujita et al., 2014.

claim: Nrf2−/− mice develop NASH on a high-fat diet.
source: Mice that lack Nrf1 in the liver develop non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) that progresses to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), and Nrf2−/− mice develop NASH on a high-fat diet (Xu et al., 2005; Okada et al., 2013; Tsujita et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Xu et al., 2005; Okada et al., 2013; Tsujita et al., 2014.

claim: Reduced Nrf protein function is thought to predispose to NASH by impairing hepatic stress resistance.
source: However, reduced Nrf protein function is thought to predispose to NASH by impairing hepatic stress resistance (Xu et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Xu et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2013.

claim: glp-1(ts) mutants at 25°C are sterile.
source: glp-1(ts) mutants that undergo larval development at the non-permissive temperature of 25°C (GSC(−) animals) are sterile, exhibit a markedly reduced number of GSCs, and live considerably longer than wild type (WT) controls (Arantes-Oliveira et al., 2002) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Arantes-Oliveira et al., 2002.

claim: glp-1(ts) mutants at 25°C exhibit a markedly reduced number of GSCs.
source: glp-1(ts) mutants that undergo larval development at the non-permissive temperature of 25°C (GSC(−) animals) are sterile, exhibit a markedly reduced number of GSCs, and live considerably longer than wild type (WT) controls (Arantes-Oliveira et al., 2002) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Arantes-Oliveira et al., 2002.

claim: glp-1(ts) mutants at 25°C live considerably longer than wild type controls.
source: glp-1(ts) mutants that undergo larval development at the non-permissive temperature of 25°C (GSC(−) animals) are sterile, exhibit a markedly reduced number of GSCs, and live considerably longer than wild type (WT) controls (Arantes-Oliveira et al., 2002) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Arantes-Oliveira et al., 2002, as well as data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The lifespan extension of glp-1(ts) mutants was blocked in a skn-1 mutant background.
source: By contrast, this lifespan extension was blocked in a skn-1 mutant background (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Lack of skn-1 impaired lifespan extension when glp-1(ts) animals were downshifted to 20°C after development was complete.
source: Lack of skn-1 also impaired lifespan extension when glp-1(ts) animals were downshifted to 20°C after development was complete (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: In GSC(-) animals, skn-1 is required for GSC inhibition to increase oxidative stress resistance.
source: In contrast to daf-16, skn-1 was also required for GSC inhibition to increase oxidative stress resistance (Figure 1C–F; Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1C-F and Table 2.

claim: The levels of SKN-1::GFP in intestinal nuclei were notably elevated in GSC(-) animals.
source: The levels of a SKN-1::GFP (green fluorescent protein) fusion in intestinal nuclei were also notably elevated in GSC(−) animals (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: SKN-1 nuclear accumulation in GSC(-) animals was associated with increased expression of direct SKN-1 target genes.
source: This was associated with increased expression of direct SKN-1 target genes, apparently through activation of their intestinal expression (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: KRI-1/KRIT1 and TCER-1/TCERG1 are required for GSC absence to induce DAF-16 nuclear accumulation and extend lifespan.
source: The KRI-1/KRIT1 ankyrin repeat protein and the TCER-1/TCERG1 transcription factor are required for GSC absence to induce DAF-16 nuclear accumulation and extend lifespan (Berman and Kenyon, 2006; Ghazi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to Berman and Kenyon, 2006; Ghazi et al., 2009.

claim: In GSC(-) animals, SKN-1 nuclear accumulation was only partially or minimally affected by loss of kri-1 or tcer-1, respectively.
source: In contrast, in GSC(−) animals SKN-1 nuclear accumulation was only partially or minimally affected by loss of kri-1 or tcer-1, respectively, but was abolished by knockdown of the pmk-1/p38 kinase (Figure 2F,G), which phosphorylates SKN-1 and under most circumstances is required for SKN-1 nuclear accumulation (Inoue et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: In GSC(-) animals, SKN-1 nuclear accumulation was abolished by knockdown of the pmk-1/p38 kinase.
source: In contrast, in GSC(−) animals SKN-1 nuclear accumulation was only partially or minimally affected by loss of kri-1 or tcer-1, respectively, but was abolished by knockdown of the pmk-1/p38 kinase (Figure 2F,G), which phosphorylates SKN-1 and under most circumstances is required for SKN-1 nuclear accumulation (Inoue et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2F,G and citation to Inoue et al., 2005.

claim: pmk-1/p38 kinase phosphorylates SKN-1.
source: In contrast, in GSC(−) animals SKN-1 nuclear accumulation was only partially or minimally affected by loss of kri-1 or tcer-1, respectively, but was abolished by knockdown of the pmk-1/p38 kinase (Figure 2F,G), which phosphorylates SKN-1 and under most circumstances is required for SKN-1 nuclear accumulation (Inoue et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Inoue et al., 2005.

claim: pmk-1/p38 kinase is required for SKN-1 nuclear accumulation under most circumstances.
source: In contrast, in GSC(−) animals SKN-1 nuclear accumulation was only partially or minimally affected by loss of kri-1 or tcer-1, respectively, but was abolished by knockdown of the pmk-1/p38 kinase (Figure 2F,G), which phosphorylates SKN-1 and under most circumstances is required for SKN-1 nuclear accumulation (Inoue et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Inoue et al., 2005.

claim: In GSC(-) animals, DAF-12 is needed for DAF-16 nuclear accumulation and activity.
source: In GSC(−) animals, DAF-12 is needed for DAF-16 nuclear accumulation and activity (Berman and Kenyon, 2006; Kenyon, 2010; Antebi, 2013), and induces expression of the microRNAs mir-84 and mir-241, which target inhibitors of DAF-16 (Shen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to Berman and Kenyon, 2006; Kenyon, 2010; Antebi, 2013.

claim: DAF-12 induces expression of the microRNAs mir-84 and mir-241, which target inhibitors of DAF-16.
source: In GSC(−) animals, DAF-12 is needed for DAF-16 nuclear accumulation and activity (Berman and Kenyon, 2006; Kenyon, 2010; Antebi, 2013), and induces expression of the microRNAs mir-84 and mir-241, which target inhibitors of DAF-16 (Shen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Shen et al., 2012.

claim: In GSC(-) animals, daf-12 knockdown only mildly affected SKN-1::GFP accumulation.
source: In GSC(−) animals, daf-12 knockdown only mildly affected SKN-1::GFP accumulation (Figure 2G), and SKN-1 target gene induction was generally not impaired by daf-12 or mir-241;mir-84 mutations (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: In GSC(-) animals, SKN-1 target gene induction was generally not impaired by daf-12 or mir-241;mir-84 mutations.
source: In GSC(−) animals, daf-12 knockdown only mildly affected SKN-1::GFP accumulation (Figure 2G), and SKN-1 target gene induction was generally not impaired by daf-12 or mir-241;mir-84 mutations (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The absence of GSCs activates SKN-1 in the intestine through a different mechanism from DAF-16.
source: The absence of GSCs therefore activates SKN-1 in the intestine but through a different mechanism from DAF-16.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion drawn from the differential requirements for kri-1, tcer-1, daf-12, and mir-241;mir-84 in regulating SKN-1 versus DAF-16.

claim: In GSC(-) animals, 1306 genes were upregulated more than fourfold.
source: In GSC(−) animals, 1306 and 615 genes were upregulated more than fourfold and fivefold, respectively, indicating a broad remodeling of transcription (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: In GSC(-) animals, 615 genes were upregulated more than fivefold.
source: In GSC(−) animals, 1306 and 615 genes were upregulated more than fourfold and fivefold, respectively, indicating a broad remodeling of transcription (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Collagen genes were the most prominently overrepresented category in genes upregulated more than fivefold in GSC(-) animals.
source: In the latter set, which is more amenable to functional annotation analysis because of its smaller size, the most prominently overrepresented category was collagen (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Collagens are generally overrepresented in other longevity-associated gene sets.
source: Although collagens may be expressed primarily in the soma, this overrepresentation is likely to be meaningful because of the extent to which these genes were upregulated (Supplementary file 1a), and because collagens are generally overrepresented in other longevity-associated gene sets, with certain collagens being critical for lifespan extension (Ewald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Ewald et al., 2015.

claim: Certain collagens are critical for lifespan extension.
source: Although collagens may be expressed primarily in the soma, this overrepresentation is likely to be meaningful because of the extent to which these genes were upregulated (Supplementary file 1a), and because collagens are generally overrepresented in other longevity-associated gene sets, with certain collagens being critical for lifespan extension (Ewald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Ewald et al., 2015.

claim: Genes involved in detoxification were notably upregulated in GSC(-) animals.
source: Also, notably upregulated in GSC(−) animals were genes involved in detoxification, immunity (C-type lectin and galectin), and metabolism, particularly FA oxidation and other lipid metabolism processes (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Genes involved in immunity (C-type lectin and galectin) were notably upregulated in GSC(-) animals.
source: Also, notably upregulated in GSC(−) animals were genes involved in detoxification, immunity (C-type lectin and galectin), and metabolism, particularly FA oxidation and other lipid metabolism processes (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Genes involved in FA oxidation and other lipid metabolism processes were notably upregulated in GSC(-) animals.
source: Also, notably upregulated in GSC(−) animals were genes involved in detoxification, immunity (C-type lectin and galectin), and metabolism, particularly FA oxidation and other lipid metabolism processes (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: skn-1 RNAi reduced expression of 87 genes that were upregulated at least fourfold in glp-1(ts) compared to WT.
source: Accordingly, skn-1 RNAi reduced expression of 87 genes that were upregulated at least fourfold in glp-1(ts) compared to WT (Figure 3D,E; Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3D,E and Supplementary file 1d.

claim: Many of the 87 skn-1-dependent GSC(-) genes appear to be direct SKN-1 targets.
source: Many of these skn-1-dependent GSC(−) genes appear to be direct SKN-1 targets, as predicted by presence of SKN-1 binding sites in their upstream regions and direct binding of SKN-1 in genome-wide chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) surveys (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Supplementary file 1d.

claim: SKN-1 maintains proteasome gene expression in WT C. elegans.
source: We re-examined this question because SKN-1 maintains proteasome gene expression and intestinal proteasome activity in WT C. elegans (Li et al., 2011), and because proteasome genes were prominent in the SKN-1-upregulated GSC(−) gene set (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Li et al., 2011.

claim: SKN-1 maintains intestinal proteasome activity in WT C. elegans.
source: We re-examined this question because SKN-1 maintains proteasome gene expression and intestinal proteasome activity in WT C. elegans (Li et al., 2011), and because proteasome genes were prominent in the SKN-1-upregulated GSC(−) gene set (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Li et al., 2011.

claim: The relative levels of proteasome subunit mRNAs were lower in GSC(-) animals.
source: In general, and consistent with previous findings (Vilchez et al., 2012), the relative levels of proteasome subunit mRNAs were lower in GSC(−) animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), possibly because of the lack of germ cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and citation to Vilchez et al., 2012.

claim: In both WT and GSC(-) animals, skn-1 knockdown comparably decreased expression of 19S and 20S proteasome subunit genes.
source: In both WT and GSC(−) animals, skn-1 knockdown comparably decreased expression of 19S and 20S proteasome subunit genes (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), the majority of which appear to be direct transcriptional targets of SKN-1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The majority of proteasome subunit genes appear to be direct transcriptional targets of SKN-1.
source: In both WT and GSC(−) animals, skn-1 knockdown comparably decreased expression of 19S and 20S proteasome subunit genes (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), the majority of which appear to be direct transcriptional targets of SKN-1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In GSC(-) animals, the lack of skn-1 dramatically reduced proteasome activity at days 1 and 5 of adulthood.
source: As these findings would predict, in GSC(−) animals, the lack of skn-1 dramatically reduced proteasome activity at days 1 and 5 of adulthood (Figure 4C,D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-G.

claim: The increased proteasome activity of GSC(-) animals is thought to derive from DAF-16-dependent transcriptional upregulation of the RPN-6.1/PSMD11 subunit.
source: The increased proteasome activity of GSC(−) animals is thought to derive from DAF-16-dependent transcriptional upregulation of the RPN-6.1/PSMD11 subunit, which connects the 19S and 20S proteasome particles (Vilchez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Vilchez et al., 2012.

claim: RPN-6.1/PSMD11 connects the 19S and 20S proteasome particles.
source: The increased proteasome activity of GSC(−) animals is thought to derive from DAF-16-dependent transcriptional upregulation of the RPN-6.1/PSMD11 subunit, which connects the 19S and 20S proteasome particles (Vilchez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Vilchez et al., 2012.

claim: rpn-6.1 is unique among proteasome subunit genes in that its mRNA levels are proportionally higher in GSC(-) animals.
source: rpn-6.1 appears to be unique among proteasome subunit genes, in that its mRNA levels are proportionally higher in GSC(−) animals (Vilchez et al., 2012) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4E and citation to Vilchez et al., 2012.

claim: skn-1 was required for increased rpn-6.1 expression in GSC(-) animals.
source: skn-1 was required for this increased rpn-6.1 expression (Figure 4E), and binding site and ChIP studies suggested that rpn-6.1 is upregulated directly by both SKN-1 and DAF-16 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: rpn-6.1 is upregulated directly by both SKN-1 and DAF-16.
source: skn-1 was required for this increased rpn-6.1 expression (Figure 4E), and binding site and ChIP studies suggested that rpn-6.1 is upregulated directly by both SKN-1 and DAF-16 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: By promoting expression of multiple proteasome subunit genes, including rpn-6.1, SKN-1 plays a central role in the increased proteasome activity that results from GSC loss.
source: We conclude that by promoting expression of multiple proteasome subunit genes, including rpn-6.1, SKN-1 plays a central role in the increased proteasome activity that results from GSC loss.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing SKN-1's effects on proteasome gene expression and activity.

claim: Genetic GSC inhibition increased expression of lipid metabolism genes that represent a wide range of processes.
source: Genetic GSC inhibition increased expression of lipid metabolism genes that represent a wide range of processes, including FFA formation from triglyceride lipolysis, as well as FA oxidation, desaturation, and elongation (Figure 5A; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5A and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Many lipid metabolism genes upregulated by GSC inhibition were also upregulated by SKN-1.
source: Many of these genes were also upregulated by SKN-1 (Figure 5A; Supplementary file 1a–c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5A and Supplementary files 1a-c.

claim: The high-confidence GSC(-) and SKN-1-upregulated gene set included the conserved lysosomal triglyceride lipase lipl-3.
source: Of particular note, the high-confidence GSC(−) and SKN-1-upregulated gene set included the conserved lysosomal triglyceride lipase lipl-3, which increases C. elegans lifespan when overexpressed and is normally induced by fasting (O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013.

claim: lipl-3 increases C. elegans lifespan when overexpressed.
source: Of particular note, the high-confidence GSC(−) and SKN-1-upregulated gene set included the conserved lysosomal triglyceride lipase lipl-3, which increases C. elegans lifespan when overexpressed and is normally induced by fasting (O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013.

claim: lipl-3 is normally induced by fasting.
source: Of particular note, the high-confidence GSC(−) and SKN-1-upregulated gene set included the conserved lysosomal triglyceride lipase lipl-3, which increases C. elegans lifespan when overexpressed and is normally induced by fasting (O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013.

claim: Ablation of skn-1 by either mutation or RNAi significantly increased lipid levels in either WT or GSC(-) day-1 adults.
source: Remarkably, ablation of skn-1 by either mutation or RNAi significantly increased lipid levels in either WT or GSC(−) day-1 adults, so that glp-1(ts);skn-1(−) animals exhibited markedly high levels of ORO staining (Figure 5B,C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: glp-1(ts);skn-1(-) animals exhibited markedly high levels of ORO staining.
source: Remarkably, ablation of skn-1 by either mutation or RNAi significantly increased lipid levels in either WT or GSC(−) day-1 adults, so that glp-1(ts);skn-1(−) animals exhibited markedly high levels of ORO staining (Figure 5B,C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: DHS-3 localizes almost exclusively to intestinal lipid droplets.
source: Proteomic and microscopy analyses have shown that DHS-3 localizes almost exclusively to intestinal lipid droplets (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) and marks the vast majority of these lipid droplets in vivo (Zhang et al., 2012; Na et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and citations to Zhang et al., 2012; Na et al., 2015.

claim: DHS-3 marks the vast majority of intestinal lipid droplets in vivo.
source: Proteomic and microscopy analyses have shown that DHS-3 localizes almost exclusively to intestinal lipid droplets (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) and marks the vast majority of these lipid droplets in vivo (Zhang et al., 2012; Na et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2012; Na et al., 2015.

claim: Lack of skn-1 increased accumulation of DHS-3::GFP in the intestine in WT and GSC(-) animals.
source: Consistent with ORO staining, lack of skn-1 increased accumulation of a DHS-3::GFP fusion in the intestine in WT and GSC(−) animals, without affecting expression of the dhs-3 mRNA (Figure 5—figure supplements 2B,C, 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 2B,C, 3.

claim: Lack of skn-1 did not affect expression of the dhs-3 mRNA.
source: Consistent with ORO staining, lack of skn-1 increased accumulation of a DHS-3::GFP fusion in the intestine in WT and GSC(−) animals, without affecting expression of the dhs-3 mRNA (Figure 5—figure supplements 2B,C, 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 2B,C, 3.

claim: SKN-1 reduces the overall level of fat accumulation.
source: An analysis of total triglyceride levels also indicated that SKN-1 reduces the overall level of fat accumulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: DAF-16 increases lipid accumulation in response to reduced IIS.
source: DAF-16 increases lipid accumulation in response to reduced IIS, and influences expression of some lipid metabolism genes in response to GSC removal (Wang et al., 2008; McCormick et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to Wang et al., 2008; McCormick et al., 2012.

claim: DAF-16 influences expression of some lipid metabolism genes in response to GSC removal.
source: DAF-16 increases lipid accumulation in response to reduced IIS, and influences expression of some lipid metabolism genes in response to GSC removal (Wang et al., 2008; McCormick et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to Wang et al., 2008; McCormick et al., 2012.

claim: Loss of daf-16 did not substantially affect overall fat storage in GSC(-) animals.
source: However, consistent with a previous study (O'Rourke et al., 2009), we found that loss of daf-16 did not substantially affect overall fat storage in GSC(−) animals (Figure 5D,E, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5D,E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, as well as citation to O'Rourke et al., 2009.

claim: SKN-1 is required to prevent excess fat accumulation under normal feeding conditions.
source: Together, our data indicate that SKN-1 is required to prevent excess fat accumulation under normal feeding conditions, and that SKN-1 but not DAF-16 reduces the lipid load that accumulates in response to GSC loss.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing SKN-1's effects on fat accumulation.

claim: SKN-1 but not DAF-16 reduces the lipid load that accumulates in response to GSC loss.
source: Together, our data indicate that SKN-1 is required to prevent excess fat accumulation under normal feeding conditions, and that SKN-1 but not DAF-16 reduces the lipid load that accumulates in response to GSC loss.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing SKN-1 and DAF-16 effects on fat accumulation.

claim: GSC ablation or inhibition prevents formation of oocytes, which endocytose lipid-rich yolk that is synthesized in the intestine.
source: However, GSC ablation or inhibition prevents formation of oocytes, which endocytose lipid-rich yolk that is synthesized in the intestine (Grant and Hirsh, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Grant and Hirsh, 1999.

claim: Fat storage might be increased indirectly by GSC loss, through accumulation of unused yolk lipids.
source: Fat storage might therefore be increased indirectly by GSC loss, through accumulation of unused yolk lipids.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a hypothesis based on the observation that GSC loss prevents oocyte formation and yolk consumption.

claim: VIT-2::GFP accumulated to extremely high levels throughout the body cavity in the absence of GSCs.
source: VIT-2::GFP was visible primarily in oocytes and embryos in WT day-1 adults but accumulated to extremely high levels throughout the body cavity in the absence of GSCs (Figure 6A,B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Yolk production was not slowed sufficiently to compensate for the lack of gametogenesis in GSC(-) animals.
source: Apparently, yolk production was not slowed sufficiently to compensate for the lack of gametogenesis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference based on the observation of high yolk accumulation in GSC(-) animals.

claim: The failure to consume yolk-associated lipid could account for the increase in overall fat storage seen in GSC(-) animals.
source: The failure to consume yolk-associated lipid could account for the increase in overall fat storage seen in GSC(−) animals.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference based on the observation of yolk accumulation in GSC(-) animals.

claim: When the oocyte-specific yolk receptor rme-2 is knocked down, yolk accumulates to high levels.
source: Supporting this idea, when the oocyte-specific yolk receptor rme-2 is knocked down, yolk accumulates to high levels (Grant and Hirsh, 1999), and in the intestine, SKN-1 accumulates in nuclei and its target gene gst-4 is activated (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Grant and Hirsh, 1999.

claim: When rme-2 is knocked down, SKN-1 accumulates in intestinal nuclei.
source: Supporting this idea, when the oocyte-specific yolk receptor rme-2 is knocked down, yolk accumulates to high levels (Grant and Hirsh, 1999), and in the intestine, SKN-1 accumulates in nuclei and its target gene gst-4 is activated (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6C-F.

claim: When rme-2 is knocked down, the SKN-1 target gene gst-4 is activated in the intestine.
source: Supporting this idea, when the oocyte-specific yolk receptor rme-2 is knocked down, yolk accumulates to high levels (Grant and Hirsh, 1999), and in the intestine, SKN-1 accumulates in nuclei and its target gene gst-4 is activated (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6C-F.

claim: rme-2 RNAi increased stress resistance in a skn-1-dependent manner.
source: Additionally, rme-2 RNAi increased stress resistance in a skn-1-dependent manner (Figure 6G and Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6G and Table 2.

claim: When de novo lipogenesis was prevented by knockdown of sbp-1, SKN-1::GFP failed to accumulate in intestinal nuclei in response to GSC inhibition.
source: When de novo lipogenesis was prevented by knockdown of the SREBP1 ortholog sbp-1 (Yang et al., 2006), SKN-1::GFP failed to accumulate in intestinal nuclei in response to GSC inhibition (Figure 6H,I), but not oxidative stress (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) or reduced IIS (daf-2 mutants, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6H,I and citation to Yang et al., 2006.

claim: sbp-1 knockdown did not prevent SKN-1::GFP accumulation in response to oxidative stress.
source: When de novo lipogenesis was prevented by knockdown of the SREBP1 ortholog sbp-1 (Yang et al., 2006), SKN-1::GFP failed to accumulate in intestinal nuclei in response to GSC inhibition (Figure 6H,I), but not oxidative stress (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) or reduced IIS (daf-2 mutants, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: sbp-1 knockdown did not prevent SKN-1::GFP accumulation in response to reduced IIS (daf-2 mutants).
source: When de novo lipogenesis was prevented by knockdown of the SREBP1 ortholog sbp-1 (Yang et al., 2006), SKN-1::GFP failed to accumulate in intestinal nuclei in response to GSC inhibition (Figure 6H,I), but not oxidative stress (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) or reduced IIS (daf-2 mutants, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The sbp-1 lipogenesis defect can be rescued by supplementation with 600 µM oleic acid.
source: The sbp-1 lipogenesis defect can be rescued by supplementation with 600 µM OA (Yang et al., 2006), which is the most abundant FA in olive oil, chicken egg yolk, and human adipose tissue (National Research Council, 1976; Kokatnur et al., 1979).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Yang et al., 2006.

claim: Oleic acid is the most abundant FA in olive oil, chicken egg yolk, and human adipose tissue.
source: The sbp-1 lipogenesis defect can be rescued by supplementation with 600 µM OA (Yang et al., 2006), which is the most abundant FA in olive oil, chicken egg yolk, and human adipose tissue (National Research Council, 1976; Kokatnur et al., 1979).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to National Research Council, 1976; Kokatnur et al., 1979.

claim: The abundance of oleic acid is increased in GSC(-) animals.
source: In C. elegans, the abundance of OA is increased in GSC(−) animals, and its synthesis by the FA desaturases, FAT-6 and FAT-7 (SCD orthologs), is required for GSC(−) lifespan extension (Goudeau et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Goudeau et al., 2011.

claim: Synthesis of oleic acid by the FA desaturases FAT-6 and FAT-7 is required for GSC(-) lifespan extension.
source: In C. elegans, the abundance of OA is increased in GSC(−) animals, and its synthesis by the FA desaturases, FAT-6 and FAT-7 (SCD orthologs), is required for GSC(−) lifespan extension (Goudeau et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Goudeau et al., 2011.

claim: fat-6/7 were required for SKN-1 to accumulate in nuclei after GSC inhibition.
source: fat-6/7 were also required for SKN-1 to accumulate in nuclei after GSC inhibition (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: In GSC(-) animals subjected to sbp-1 RNAi, SKN-1 nuclear accumulation was fully restored by OA supplementation.
source: Moreover, in GSC(−) animals subjected to sbp-1 RNAi, SKN-1 nuclear accumulation was fully restored by OA supplementation (Figure 6H,I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6H,I.

claim: sbp-1 and fat-6/7 were required for GSC absence to increase stress resistance.
source: Consistent with their importance for SKN-1 function, sbp-1 and fat-6/7 were required for GSC absence to increase stress resistance (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Certain unsaturated lipids are required for SKN-1 to be activated in response to GSC loss, but not necessarily by other stimuli.
source: Together, our data suggest that certain unsaturated lipids are required for SKN-1 to be activated in response to GSC loss, but not necessarily by other stimuli, and therefore, that lipid accumulation per se might activate SKN-1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing differential requirements for lipids in SKN-1 activation by different stimuli.

claim: Lipid accumulation per se might activate SKN-1.
source: Together, our data suggest that certain unsaturated lipids are required for SKN-1 to be activated in response to GSC loss, but not necessarily by other stimuli, and therefore, that lipid accumulation per se might activate SKN-1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a speculation based on the observation that lipid-related interventions affect SKN-1 activation.

claim: Feeding of either oleic acid or coconut oil activated gst-4 in WT animals in a skn-1-dependent manner without impairing development or reproduction.
source: Accordingly, feeding of either OA- or coconut oil (CO)-activated gst-4 in WT animals in a skn-1-dependent manner without impairing development or reproduction (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-E.

claim: CO feeding strongly induced nuclear accumulation of SKN-1 but not DAF-16.
source: CO feeding strongly induced nuclear accumulation of SKN-1 but not DAF-16 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F,G), and sbp-1 RNAi did not impair DAF-16 nuclear accumulation in GSC(−) animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 2H,I), supporting the notion that GSCs regulate SKN-1 and DAF-16 differently.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2F,G.

claim: sbp-1 RNAi did not impair DAF-16 nuclear accumulation in GSC(-) animals.
source: CO feeding strongly induced nuclear accumulation of SKN-1 but not DAF-16 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F,G), and sbp-1 RNAi did not impair DAF-16 nuclear accumulation in GSC(−) animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 2H,I), supporting the notion that GSCs regulate SKN-1 and DAF-16 differently.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2H,I.

claim: GSCs regulate SKN-1 and DAF-16 differently.
source: CO feeding strongly induced nuclear accumulation of SKN-1 but not DAF-16 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F,G), and sbp-1 RNAi did not impair DAF-16 nuclear accumulation in GSC(−) animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 2H,I), supporting the notion that GSCs regulate SKN-1 and DAF-16 differently.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of lipid-related interventions on SKN-1 versus DAF-16.

claim: Oxidative stress induced by sodium arsenite robustly activates the p38/PMK-1 kinase through phosphorylation, leading in turn to SKN-1 activation.
source: Oxidative stress induced by sodium arsenite (AS) robustly activates the p38/PMK-1 kinase through phosphorylation, leading in turn to SKN-1 activation (Inoue et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Inoue et al., 2005.

claim: GSC loss induced SKN-1 nuclear accumulation at least as dramatically as AS treatment.
source: GSC loss induced SKN-1 nuclear accumulation at least as dramatically as AS treatment (Figure 2B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) but did not detectably increase PMK-1/p38 activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 2J), suggesting that any stress arising from the lack of GSCs might not be sufficient on its own to explain SKN-1 activation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: GSC loss did not detectably increase PMK-1/p38 activity.
source: GSC loss induced SKN-1 nuclear accumulation at least as dramatically as AS treatment (Figure 2B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) but did not detectably increase PMK-1/p38 activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 2J), suggesting that any stress arising from the lack of GSCs might not be sufficient on its own to explain SKN-1 activation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2J.

claim: Any stress arising from the lack of GSCs might not be sufficient on its own to explain SKN-1 activation.
source: GSC loss induced SKN-1 nuclear accumulation at least as dramatically as AS treatment (Figure 2B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) but did not detectably increase PMK-1/p38 activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 2J), suggesting that any stress arising from the lack of GSCs might not be sufficient on its own to explain SKN-1 activation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference based on the observation that GSC loss does not increase PMK-1/p38 activity despite inducing SKN-1 nuclear accumulation.

claim: The lysosomal lipases LIPL-1/3 and LIPL-4 enable production of specific unsaturated FFAs that promote autophagy and longevity by breaking down triglycerides.
source: By breaking down triglycerides, the lysosomal lipases LIPL-1/3 and LIPL-4 enable production of specific unsaturated FFAs that promote autophagy and longevity (Lapierre et al., 2011; O'Rourke et al., 2013; O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013; Folick et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to Lapierre et al., 2011; O'Rourke et al., 2013; O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013; Folick et al., 2015.

claim: LBP-8/FABP1 escorts some FAs from the lysosome to the nucleus.
source: Some of these FAs are escorted from the lysosome to the nucleus by the conserved lipid-binding protein LBP-8/FABP1 (Folick et al., 2015; Han and Brunet, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to Folick et al., 2015; Han and Brunet, 2015.

claim: In GSC(-) animals, SKN-1 nuclear accumulation was inhibited modestly by lipl-4 RNAi but more strongly by lipl-1/3 double knockdown.
source: In GSC(−) animals, SKN-1 nuclear accumulation was inhibited modestly by lipl-4 RNAi but more strongly by lipl-1/3 double knockdown (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: lipl-3 RNAi reduced stress resistance in GSC(-) but not WT animals.
source: Furthermore, lipl-3 RNAi reduced stress resistance in GSC(−) but not WT animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Fat storage is increased in lipl-1/3 mutants.
source: Given that fat storage is increased in lipl-1/3 mutants (O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013), our data suggest that in GSC(−) animals, SKN-1 activity may depend upon particular lipl-1/3-dependent products, not lipid levels per se.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013.

claim: In GSC(-) animals, SKN-1 activity may depend upon particular lipl-1/3-dependent products, not lipid levels per se.
source: Given that fat storage is increased in lipl-1/3 mutants (O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013), our data suggest that in GSC(−) animals, SKN-1 activity may depend upon particular lipl-1/3-dependent products, not lipid levels per se.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference based on the observation that lipl-1/3 knockdown reduces SKN-1 activity despite increasing fat storage.

claim: Knockdown of lbp-8 or other LBPs interfered with SKN-1::GFP nuclear accumulation in GSC(-) animals.
source: Knockdown of lbp-8 or other LBPs also interfered with SKN-1::GFP nuclear accumulation in GSC(−) animals, and lbp-8 RNAi impaired SKN-1-dependent gst-4 activation by OA, indicating involvement of FA transport (Figure 6J,K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6J,K.

claim: lbp-8 RNAi impaired SKN-1-dependent gst-4 activation by OA.
source: Knockdown of lbp-8 or other LBPs also interfered with SKN-1::GFP nuclear accumulation in GSC(−) animals, and lbp-8 RNAi impaired SKN-1-dependent gst-4 activation by OA, indicating involvement of FA transport (Figure 6J,K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6J,K.

claim: In GSC(-) animals, excessive lipid levels lead to production of OA- and LIPL-1/3-dependent FAs that activate SKN-1, possibly through FA-based signaling.
source: Together, our data suggest that in GSC(−) animals, excessive lipid levels lead to production of OA- and LIPL-1/3-dependent FAs that activate SKN-1, possibly through FA-based signaling (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by the model shown in Figure 7.

claim: SKN-1 is required for lifespan to be extended by reduced insulin/IGF-1 signaling.
source: Previous work showed that SKN-1 is required for lifespan to be extended by reduced insulin/IGF-1, mTORC1, or mTORC2 signaling, by dietary restriction and by low-level mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production (Bishop and Guarente, 2007; Tullet et al., 2008; Robida-Stubbs et al., 2012; Zarse et al., 2012; Schmeisser et al., 2013; Mizunuma et al., 2014; Moroz et al., 2014; Ewald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: SKN-1 is required for lifespan to be extended by reduced mTORC1 signaling.
source: Previous work showed that SKN-1 is required for lifespan to be extended by reduced insulin/IGF-1, mTORC1, or mTORC2 signaling, by dietary restriction and by low-level mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production (Bishop and Guarente, 2007; Tullet et al., 2008; Robida-Stubbs et al., 2012; Zarse et al., 2012; Schmeisser et al., 2013; Mizunuma et al., 2014; Moroz et al., 2014; Ewald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: SKN-1 is required for lifespan to be extended by reduced mTORC2 signaling.
